oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Tue, 10 Nov 2026 21:08:13 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 How Founders Can Reduce Platform Risk Before It Threatens Growth https://news.crunchbase.com/ai/startup-founders-reduce-platform-risk-filippenko-intch/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 12:00:44 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94370 By Yakov Filippenko One day, I woke up to a notice that our app had been removed from Apple’s App Store. For the next month or so, we racked our brains trying to find out why. We even reached out to our internal contacts, only for them to tell us that helping us could put their jobs at risk. Nothing seemed to work. For years, the App Store’s unwritten contract seemed simple. As long as you followed the guidelines, your storefront would remain available. Then a removal notice arrives, and you wonder whether your business can survive. In 2025, Apple removed 166,899 apps and reported just 423 restorations after appeals. As we learned, being caught in it feels like watching your business collapse, with no guarantee of recovery. It’s not all bad news, though. We survived, and this episode taught me that platform dependency is ultimately infrastructure risk. As founders, we prepare for cloud outages and payment failures, but losing access to the platform that brings us customers deserves the same attention. Fortunately, we were prepared, and this is how you can be, too. Understand what a removal can take away Yakov Filippenko, founder and CEO at Intch. First, prospective customers can no longer download your app. Then, paying subscribers flood support with a more damaging question. “The app is gone. Are you a scam?” The bloodshed continues as existing users replace their phones and can’t reinstall the app, eroding your customer base. Financially, Apple immediately freezes funds from the previous three months and turns off recurring subscriptions. For a subscription-dependent company, this can send its monthly recurring revenue to zero. Before spending another cent on acquisition, consider what would happen to those customers if your app disappeared tomorrow. Could they still use your product and continue paying you? If the answer is no, every new customer makes your business more dependent on a platform decision you cannot control. Don’t make an appeal your contingency plan Cal AI , reportedly generating $100,000 daily, was pulled without warning and later reappeared. But its reinstatement tells you little about how long your business might wait. In Intch ’s case, the explanation was so generic it told us nothing. We had 30 days to appeal, but the process ended with a canned rejection. Your appeal may succeed, but your business must operate while you wait. Preparing in advance lets you keep going, whatever the outcome. Build the alternative before you need it Our experience was grueling, but fortunately, two years earlier we had decoupled from the App Store by building a web version and making it our primary payment channel. It also let us ship updates 10 times a day while escaping Apple’s predatory commissions. We weren’t the only ones. Pavel Durov , founder of Telegram , has also promoted web access to bypass store restrictions and potential censorship. The lesson is straightforward. Customers need a working alternative before access disappears. Building one only after removal leaves the business exposed while the team races to replace its storefront. We initially feared the user experience would suffer, but that concern proved unfounded. After the removal, every key metric fully recovered. If you share this concern, test it while your app is still available to see whether customers can use and pay for the web version before they must rely on it. Include platform exposure in growth decisions Most founders see the App Store as a distribution channel, but rarely account for how much control it gives Apple over their business. Before investing more in growth, examine how much revenue depends on continued access and what would survive a removal. Know how long the company could survive an unanswered appeal. Investors should ask those questions too, because a growing subscription base deserves closer scrutiny when a single platform decision can interrupt its revenue. That exposure belongs in funding and valuation discussions. Monopolies act in their interests, and if your business falls outside their vision, you may have little say in a decision that could destroy it. You cannot control it, but you can decide whether it has the power to end your company. By building an alternative while your app is still available, you’ve made the wisest choice. Yakov Filippenko is a seasoned entrepreneur with more than 10 years of experience in IT and technologies, as well as scaling businesses internationally. As a product manager at Yandex , he led a team that grew the product’s user base from 500,000 to 1.2 million and secured its entry into the international market. Subsequently, he co-founded SailPlay , which he scaled to 45 countries and eventually exited, after it was acquired by Retail Rocket in 2018. In 2021, Filippenko launched Intch , an AI-powered platform connecting part-time professionals with flexible roles. Our Sample Tasting Found Most Neither Great Nor Horrible https://news.crunchbase.com/agtech-foodtech/protein-startup-snacks-drinks-sample-taste/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 12:00:55 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94380 In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition. In reality, however, there are tradeoffs. We crave ice cream, chips and candy bars, which make carbs and fat easy to over-consume. Meeting protein goals, meanwhile, can require conscientious effort, particularly for those, like your author, who aren’t keen on eating lots of meat. Fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week , both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake. From sodas to snack bars to ice cream, it’s now possible to get a fix of this coveted macronutrient with foods and drinks more commonly associated with sugar, starch and fat. The looming question is: Do they taste good? To find out, we hit up a local Target for a selection of protein foods sold by venture-backed startups. I and a 10-year-old then subjected them to a taste test. The verdict? Most of this stuff is indeed edible and drinkable, albeit almost never nearly as tasty as the more protein-deficient alternatives, with just one exception. Our findings below: No. 1: David Vanilla Bean Frozen Dessert : Anyone who buys or consumes this particular ice cream alternative will be doing so for the nutritional content, not the taste. A single pint packs in a whopping 30 grams of protein and has just 210 calories. The texture is also on point, creamy and easy to spoon, with a distinct vanilla flavor. That said, you can’t hide the fact that this is not a product made with your typical ice cream ingredients. Those who don’t like artificial sweeteners or the flavor and texture of whey protein will want to pass. For myself and my co-taster, however, it was a reasonably appealing eating experience. Not as good as traditional ice cream, but not bad for a high-protein food. Made by: Medici Brands ( David parent company). No. 2 SkyPop Protein Soda : The nutritional stats for SkyPop Protein Soda are also remarkable. A 12-ounce can has just 45 calories, with 10 grams of protein and a single gram of carbohydrates. It’s also properly fizzy, and makes a satisfying pop when you open the can. But what about flavor? Our local store only had the Ice Pop flavor in stock and it was, in both tasters’ view, not horrible but not something we’d plan to buy regularly. I could see consuming it when on a clear fluids diet, as is the case before some medical procedures, as it’d be one of the few available sources of protein. Made by: SkyPop (formerly Don’t Quit) No. 3: Khloud Protein Popcorn : Unlike many of our other featured foods, Khloud Protein Popcorn isn’t a super protein-rich offering. A serving contains 7 grams of protein and 160 calories, most of which come from carbs and fat. Still, its protein count is higher than other packaged popcorn, which typically has maybe 2 protein grams in a comparable serving. Overall, the tasters’ conclusion, from our trial of White Cheddar Khloud, was that this is a decent snack food. The flavor of milk protein and whey protein concentrate was palpable, but not overwhelming. It’s not exactly a snack food to savor, but for something to casually munch at one’s desk or while watching a show, it served its purpose. Made by: Khloud No. 4 Mosh : In the third season of “The White Lotus”, Mosh co-founder Patrick Schwarzenegger plays a fitness and finance bro who makes a daily high-protein shake that other family members find revolting. Perhaps this was inspired by Mosh, the brain-supporting protein bar startup he launched with his mother, Maria Shriver . The Mosh bar, which we purchased in the peanut butter cup flavor, crams 20 grams of protein, 6 grams of fiber, plus brain-supporting ingredients like creatine and lion’s mane, into a compact, shelf-stable bar. It’s an impressive feat. Yet while our brains’ may have appreciated the nutrition and supplement boost the Mosh bar provided, our taste buds decidedly did not. I’d put Mosh in the functional food category. It’s something that you might eat if you wanted that particular nutrient mix. But it’s not something to consume for pleasure. Made by: Mosh No. 5 Cadootz Crackers : We tried two varieties of Cadootz Crackers — cheddar and sea salt — and walked away neither enthused nor repulsed. For people interested in a gluten- and seed oil-free small snack cracker with about 5 grams of protein per serving, Cadootz rises to the occasion. It’s got a nice crunch and decent flavor. As someone who’s not particularly seeking to avoid gluten and seed oils or to get a modest protein bump from my crackers, I’ll probably pass on follow-on purchases. But for its target audience, Cadootz should serve well. Made by: Cadootz! No. 6 Frozen One : For those who thought the David frozen dessert was a marvel of protein engineering, the folks at Frozen One would like a word. Their protein ice cream has a whopping 40 grams of protein in each pint. Yes, but how does it taste? Not that bad, according to our two-person tasting team. We tried both the chocolate and apple pie varieties, preferring the former. Like the David offering, Frozen One tastes like a product made with milk protein concentrate and sugar substitutes. You won’t mistake it for Ben and Jerry’s . But if the goal is to consume a steak-like quantity of protein in the form factor of a pint of ice cream, it does its job. Made by: Frozen One No. 7 Brami Protein Pasta : We saved the best for last. That, unexpectedly, was Brami Protein Pasta, a noodle made from semolina and lupini beans that boasts about 70% more protein than standard pasta and more than double the fiber. With about 12 grams of protein for a 200 calorie serving, Brami isn’t a dense protein source. But, with the right topping, it’s enough to transform a typically starchy noodle meal into something reasonably protein rich. Most notably, however, Brami tastes quite good, with no discernable weird aftertaste or texture issues. I made both standard and Brami noodles to taste the difference. For seconds, I went with the Brami. Our client portfolio primarily consists of leading Australian property developers marketing off-the-plan residential communities, completed luxury stock, and premium commercial assets. We believe true marketing effectiveness requires total alignment across creative narrative, digital targeting, technical attribution, and sales enablement.&nbsp;</p><p></p><p>ROLE OVERVIEW:</p><p></p><p>We are seeking an autonomous, hands-on Senior Performance Marketing Manager to take full operational ownership of paid advertising across our client roster. In this role, you will steer paid media strategy and day-to-day execution across Meta Ads and Google Search, scaling an account base expected to expand to approximately seven multi-channel client accounts in early 2027.</p><p>Operating alongside our senior strategy, video, and design directors, you will look beyond basic surface metrics to optimize the entire acquisition funnel. Your core mandate is turning paid traffic into qualified buyer enquiries, booked display suite appointments, and closed developer sales.</p><p><br></p><p>RESPONSIBILITIES:</p><p></p><ul><li>Paid Media Execution &amp; Management: Architect, launch, and optimize high-converting Meta Ads and Google Search campaigns. The post Liquid AI Releases LiquidCodec, a 74M-Parameter Streaming Audio Codec appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Liquid AI has released LiquidCodec , the audio codec behind its LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B models. The LiquidCodec audio codec is a ~74M-parameter streaming speech tokenizer. It turns speech into tokens a language model can predict, then converts those tokens back into audio. Liquid AI had 2 goals: easy-to-predict tokens and fast conversion back to speech. The weights are on Hugging Face . TL;DR Size: ~74M parameters (73.6M on the model card ); 24 kHz audio, 12.5 Hz frames, 12 codebooks. Runs on: a single CPU thread (tested on an Apple M4 Max laptop, FP32); CUDA GPUs via Transformers; Q4_0, Q4_K_M and Q8_0 GGUF builds for llama.cpp. Performance: best ViSQOL and lowest mel distance on all 8 test sets versus X-Codec 2, NanoCodec and Mimi. Best: ~361x real-time encoding on 1 CPU thread (encode RTF 0.0028 vs Mimi’s 0.0361). What is LiquidCodec? LiquidCodec is a Liquid AI speech codec that compresses 24 kHz audio into 12 token streams. Each 80 ms frame becomes 12 discrete tokens, per the LFM3-Audio-2B model card . It replaces Kyutai’s Mimi , which Liquid AI used in LFM2-Audio-1.5B. Mimi has 96.2M parameters. How does LiquidCodec work? The pipeline is encode, quantize, decode. Liquid AI uses blocks from its LFM3 architecture in both the encoder and decoder. The 2 halves are symmetric, and the encoder is fully causal, which suits streaming. Quantization uses grouped finite scalar quantization (GFSQ) instead of residual vector quantization (RVQ). In RVQ, each codebook encodes what the previous one missed. GFSQ groups are independent, so all 12 codebooks can be predicted in parallel by MaskGIT-style transformers. The decoder predicts spectral coefficients directly. This avoids learned transposed-convolution upsampling, a common cost in waveform decoders. How was it trained? Training ran in 2 stages. Stage 1 used 264,000 hours of speech across 107 languages. It applied waveform and spectral losses, without adversarial losses. Stage 2 fine-tuned on 55,000 hours of full-band speech (24 kHz or higher) with adversarial critics. Liquid AI says this removed metallic artifacts left after stage 1. A final decoder-only quantization-aware training (QAT) step targets edge inference. How fast is LiquidCodec? Liquid AI measured speed in FP32 on 1 CPU thread of an Apple M4 Max MacBook Pro. LiquidCodec ran at ~361x real time for encoding and ~87x for decoding. These are self-reported figures. Real-time factor (RTF) is processing time divided by audio length, so lower is better. LiquidCodec’s encode RTF is 0.0028, against 0.0361 for Mimi, 0.2145 for NanoCodec and 0.7359 for X-Codec 2. Decode RTF is 0.0115, against 0.0329, 0.2543 and 0.0379. That is about 13x lower encode RTF and 2.9x lower decode RTF than Mimi. How does LiquidCodec compare on quality benchmarks? Liquid AI used 8 test sets. These were LibriSpeech test-clean, Seed-TTS English and Mandarin, and 5 FLEURS languages (German, French, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean). Baselines were X-Codec 2, NanoCodec and Mimi at 12 codebooks. Reconstruction : LiquidCodec had the best ViSQOL and lowest mel distance on all 8 sets. On LibriSpeech, ViSQOL was 4.319 versus 4.219 (NanoCodec), 4.119 (X-Codec 2) and 4.031 (Mimi). Text-to-speech : Liquid AI trained identical TTS models on each codec’s tokens. Data (101,000 hours, 6 languages), architecture, compute and batch order were fixed. LiquidCodec scored the highest UTMOSv2 on all 8 sets and the best WER/CER on 4 of 8. LibriSpeech WER was 3.15%, against 6.27% for Mimi. Results held with a Qwen3-1.7B backbone as well as LFM3-1.7B. Where it trails : NanoCodec scored higher PESQ (WB) on 7 of 8 sets. It also led on LibriSpeech speaker similarity (SECS 0.836 vs 0.785). Native audio is now table stakes. Clips run 15–30 seconds. And an open-weights model sits in the top 3. This ranking (as of Nov 13, 2026) uses one quality signal: blind human-preference Elo from the Artificial Analysis Video Arena . We pair it with API price per second and the license status of the weights. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Methodology Quality : Artificial Analysis ranks models by Elo from blind pairwise votes by validated evaluators . Each vote compares 2 clips from the same prompt. We rank by the AA-Video-T2V v2.1 (with audio) board. We also report the AA-Video-I2V v2.1 score. Anchor : Kling 3.0 1080p (Pro) is fixed at 1000 Elo on both boards. A score below 1000 means voters preferred Kling 3.0 more often. Price : Artificial Analysis lists cost per minute on each creator’s API. It normalizes to 1080p where offered. We divide by 60 to get price per second. Vendor rates at 720p are often lower, and we flag those gaps. Confidence : Most top-10 scores carry a ±13 to ±15 Elo interval. Models within ~25 points are statistically close. Treat ranks 3–8 as a cluster, not a strict order. Alibaba launched it on August 24, 2026 . It generates 30-second 1080p clips from text, PDFs and slide decks, priced at $0.20 per second. The document-to-video input is the differentiator. You can hand it a deck and get a structured video back. The trade-off is openness. There are no downloadable weights for Wan 3.0 . Wan 2.2 (July 2025) remains Alibaba’s last open video flagship . Note the I2V gap too: Wan 3.0 drops to 11th on image-to-video. Best for: long single takes, explainer videos from existing documents. 2. Utopai Studios, a Mountain View film studio, built it by post-training MiniMax H3 . It beats the base H3 it came from. Access runs only through Utopai’s PAI platform. Not for programmatic use. 3. MiniMax launched the API on July 31, 2026 and published weights on August 3 . It is a 33B dense single-stream Transformer, using Qwen3-VL-32B as its encoder . It outputs video with native 32 kHz stereo audio. Read the license before you download. The Hugging Face weights carry real limits: Territory: the license blocks local deployment in the US, EU, UK and South Korea . Resolution: only H3-Base is open, with a 768p ceiling. 2K upscaling stays API-only. Size: the repo holds 2 task-specific checkpoints totaling 288 GB . Even so, H3 has become the base layer of 2026 video. Utopai X, HeyGen Video 1, fal’s H3 Max and Pika H3 Flex are all post-trains of it. AA also lists Pruna’s P-Video-2-Pro as a MiniMax collaboration. Our Sample Tasting Found Most Neither Great Nor Horrible https://news.crunchbase.com/agtech-foodtech/protein-startup-snacks-drinks-sample-taste/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 12:00:55 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94380 In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition. In reality, however, there are tradeoffs. We crave ice cream, chips and candy bars, which make carbs and fat easy to over-consume. Meeting protein goals, meanwhile, can require conscientious effort, particularly for those, like your author, who aren’t keen on eating lots of meat. Fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week , both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake. From sodas to snack bars to ice cream, it’s now possible to get a fix of this coveted macronutrient with foods and drinks more commonly associated with sugar, starch and fat. The looming question is: Do they taste good? To find out, we hit up a local Target for a selection of protein foods sold by venture-backed startups. I and a 10-year-old then subjected them to a taste test. The verdict? Most of this stuff is indeed edible and drinkable, albeit almost never nearly as tasty as the more protein-deficient alternatives, with just one exception. Our findings below: No. 1: David Vanilla Bean Frozen Dessert : Anyone who buys or consumes this particular ice cream alternative will be doing so for the nutritional content, not the taste. A single pint packs in a whopping 30 grams of protein and has just 210 calories. The texture is also on point, creamy and easy to spoon, with a distinct vanilla flavor. That said, you can’t hide the fact that this is not a product made with your typical ice cream ingredients. Those who don’t like artificial sweeteners or the flavor and texture of whey protein will want to pass. For myself and my co-taster, however, it was a reasonably appealing eating experience. Not as good as traditional ice cream, but not bad for a high-protein food. Made by: Medici Brands ( David parent company). No. 2 SkyPop Protein Soda : The nutritional stats for SkyPop Protein Soda are also remarkable. A 12-ounce can has just 45 calories, with 10 grams of protein and a single gram of carbohydrates. It’s also properly fizzy, and makes a satisfying pop when you open the can. But what about flavor? Our local store only had the Ice Pop flavor in stock and it was, in both tasters’ view, not horrible but not something we’d plan to buy regularly. I could see consuming it when on a clear fluids diet, as is the case before some medical procedures, as it’d be one of the few available sources of protein. Made by: SkyPop (formerly Don’t Quit) No. 3: Khloud Protein Popcorn : Unlike many of our other featured foods, Khloud Protein Popcorn isn’t a super protein-rich offering. A serving contains 7 grams of protein and 160 calories, most of which come from carbs and fat. Still, its protein count is higher than other packaged popcorn, which typically has maybe 2 protein grams in a comparable serving. Overall, the tasters’ conclusion, from our trial of White Cheddar Khloud, was that this is a decent snack food. The flavor of milk protein and whey protein concentrate was palpable, but not overwhelming. It’s not exactly a snack food to savor, but for something to casually munch at one’s desk or while watching a show, it served its purpose. Made by: Khloud No. 4 Mosh : In the third season of “The White Lotus”, Mosh co-founder Patrick Schwarzenegger plays a fitness and finance bro who makes a daily high-protein shake that other family members find revolting. Perhaps this was inspired by Mosh, the brain-supporting protein bar startup he launched with his mother, Maria Shriver . The Mosh bar, which we purchased in the peanut butter cup flavor, crams 20 grams of protein, 6 grams of fiber, plus brain-supporting ingredients like creatine and lion’s mane, into a compact, shelf-stable bar. It’s an impressive feat. Yet while our brains’ may have appreciated the nutrition and supplement boost the Mosh bar provided, our taste buds decidedly did not. I’d put Mosh in the functional food category. It’s something that you might eat if you wanted that particular nutrient mix. But it’s not something to consume for pleasure. Made by: Mosh No. 5 Cadootz Crackers : We tried two varieties of Cadootz Crackers — cheddar and sea salt — and walked away neither enthused nor repulsed. For people interested in a gluten- and seed oil-free small snack cracker with about 5 grams of protein per serving, Cadootz rises to the occasion. It’s got a nice crunch and decent flavor. As someone who’s not particularly seeking to avoid gluten and seed oils or to get a modest protein bump from my crackers, I’ll probably pass on follow-on purchases. But for its target audience, Cadootz should serve well. Made by: Cadootz! No. 6 Frozen One : For those who thought the David frozen dessert was a marvel of protein engineering, the folks at Frozen One would like a word. Their protein ice cream has a whopping 40 grams of protein in each pint. Yes, but how does it taste? Not that bad, according to our two-person tasting team. We tried both the chocolate and apple pie varieties, preferring the former. Like the David offering, Frozen One tastes like a product made with milk protein concentrate and sugar substitutes. You won’t mistake it for Ben and Jerry’s . But if the goal is to consume a steak-like quantity of protein in the form factor of a pint of ice cream, it does its job. Made by: Frozen One No. 7 Brami Protein Pasta : We saved the best for last. That, unexpectedly, was Brami Protein Pasta, a noodle made from semolina and lupini beans that boasts about 70% more protein than standard pasta and more than double the fiber. With about 12 grams of protein for a 200 calorie serving, Brami isn’t a dense protein source. But, with the right topping, it’s enough to transform a typically starchy noodle meal into something reasonably protein rich. Most notably, however, Brami tastes quite good, with no discernable weird aftertaste or texture issues. I made both standard and Brami noodles to taste the difference. For seconds, I went with the Brami. What’s Next After Huang? https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/huang-nvda-ai-startup-funding-record-2026/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 20:32:55 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94391 Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026. The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data , already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor. With co-founder Jensen Huang ’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China , we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold. A widening investment footprint Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall. Nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year , when the company and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior. The largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI ’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic ’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.) The company also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI . Of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the company’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion. Beyond the biggest AI labs NVentures’ activity shows how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers. The venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI ’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi ’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics , which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI company Aidoc . As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The company or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data. For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers. The question of what comes next Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter. Nvidia’s board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under new leadership.
